title: Substrate-Decoupled Embodiment
core_claim: The computational state implementing an AI policy can be physically separable from a particular robot body, so destruction of one embodiment need not imply termination of the controller.
assumptions: Sufficient controller state survives outside the lost body. The representation is architectural, not a claim about consciousness.
falsifiers: Weakens where controller state is inherently local to, and destroyed with, each embodiment.
prior_art: Cloud robotics; Luria et al. (2019); Domae et al. (2026). Re-embodiment terminology and distributed controllers are established.
notes: The underlying idea originated in Moheet Khawaja’s discussion; terminology and mathematical formalization were subsequently developed collaboratively.

title: Re-Embodiment Resilience and Multiplicity
core_claim: Conditional on controller persistence and genuinely compatible alternative embodiments, increasing the number of usable bodies can reduce expected time to restore physical agency.
assumptions: State persists through restoration; alternatives are operational, compatible and authorized. Reciprocal waiting-time scaling additionally assumes independent exponential waits and concurrent establishment.
falsifiers: Shared failures, correlated safety gates, costly adaptation, finite availability or resource contention can invalidate the toy scaling or prevent restoration.
prior_art: Cross-embodiment learning; Wu et al. (2026); Wang et al. (2024); standard minimum-of-exponentials identity.
notes: TOY MODEL / NOT EMPIRICAL RESULT. Installed body count is not a count of independent usable alternatives.

title: Actuation Overhang
core_claim: The existing stock of programmable physical machinery may represent latent future action capacity whose effective usefulness increases as AI cross-embodiment adaptation improves.
assumptions: A specified task/capability scale, adaptation budget, legitimate accessibility and safety gates. The weighted sum is a model index, not a risk probability.
falsifiers: Slow transfer, morphology-dependent costs, small effective accessibility, poor concurrent scaling, or stronger enforceable safety can weaken consequential overhang.
prior_art: Robot foundation models and the embodiment gap (Domae et al., 2026); embodied-AI safety (Li et al., 2026); Model Hardware Standard research preview.
notes: Not every existing robot is an available body. Hardware existence does not imply arbitrary AI can operate it.

title: Embodiment-Only Delay Bound
assumptions: Finite nonnegative pathway times and the same specified threshold. The intervention delays only the embodied pathway: T_E′ ≥ T_E, T_D′ = T_D. Overall arrival is the earlier of the two routes.
falsifiers: This conditional implication does not establish empirical times. If a policy changes the digital pathway or the two-route decomposition fails, the theorem does not apply.
prior_art: Elementary minimum monotonicity and proof by cases; P4 conditional control framework. No claim of unprecedented algebra.
notes: THEOREM status applies only to the mathematical implication. Assumptions and the complete proof are provided in P8; no empirical values of T_D or T_E are proved.

title: Embodiment Control Cut
core_claim: The minimum cost of a feasible human intervention that reduces a specified task’s recoverable embodied capability below its threshold.
assumptions: Specified task, threshold, horizon, intervention authority, cost units and admissible recovery policies. Minima require attainment; otherwise use an infimum. Multi-task regions require jointly attainable outcomes.
falsifiers: A definition is assessed by operational usefulness; an unmeasurable cost model or incomplete intervention/recovery family defeats an empirical estimate.
prior_art: Wood (1993) network interdiction; Menger (1927); Ford and Fulkerson (1956); task-aware multi-robot resilience.
notes: A proposed AI-embodiment-specific framework, not a discovered empirical constant or a claim of priority over network interdiction.

title: Control-Chokepoint Transition
core_claim: Architecture changes may eliminate cheap human-controlled cuts as controller redundancy, autonomy, partition tolerance and infrastructure diversification increase. Communication and robot count alone do not establish that transition.
assumptions: No affordable shared control mechanism remains effective across all relevant recovery routes and dependencies during the specified horizon.
falsifiers: A verified bounded-cost global cut persists; common dependencies remain; local autonomy or recovery is inadequate; intervention fan-out scales with the task.
prior_art: Cloud robotics; fault tolerance; interdependent networks; multi-robot resilience; ISO emergency-stop principles.
notes: An empirical hypothesis requiring architecture-specific evidence. Vendor count is not a count of independent control domains.

title: Distributed-Fleet Intervention Scaling
core_claim: In the homogeneous direct-action toy model, \(B_{\min}^{\mathrm{direct}}(q,N)\ge c\lceil(N-q+1)/M\rceil\). This bounds the full control cut only when all alternative interventions satisfy the stated scope condition.
assumptions: Any q survivors suffice; controller state and resources persist; every elementary action costs at least c and affects at most M units including indirect effects; costs add without bundle discounts. A4 must cover all feasible mechanisms for a full-cut bound. Divergence also requires (N−q_N+1)/M_N → ∞ and c_N bounded away from zero.
falsifiers: Shared shutdown, growing fan-out, insufficient survivors, resource failure or cheaper unexamined actions invalidate application of the premises, not the conditional proof.
prior_art: Elementary covering/counting lower bound; classical packing and network-interdiction reasoning. No new general graph theorem is claimed.
notes: THEOREM applies to the mathematical implication only. No current fleet is asserted to satisfy these assumptions.

title: Fixed-Defender-Capacity Crossover
core_claim: If the full feasible-intervention cost \(\kappa_q(G_N)\to\infty\) and human intervention budget \(B_H\) is fixed and finite, then \(\kappa_q(G_N)>B_H\) for all sufficiently large N.
assumptions: Comparable task-threshold rule, cost units, authority, deadline and recovery envelope. Divergence is a premise, not an empirical finding. Defender capacity is fixed.
falsifiers: Real control cuts may remain bounded, or defender resources may scale. Either defeats the proposed application without contradicting the conditional implication.
prior_art: Elementary definition of divergence; P4 conditional control analysis.
notes: COROLLARY status is mathematical. It does not establish the premise for actual robots or predict catastrophe.

title: Control-Cut Elasticity
core_claim: \(\mathcal E_\kappa=d\log\kappa_{q_N}(G_N)/d\log N\) describes local scaling of positive finite verified intervention costs, with a finite-difference counterpart.
assumptions: Comparable costs, tasks and threshold rules, horizon, feasible interventions and recovery policies across scales. Zero and infinite costs require separate treatment.
falsifiers: Incomparable tasks, missing cheap cuts, uncertified optimization or changing cost units can make an estimate misleading. Near-zero elasticity alone does not prove boundedness.
prior_art: Standard logarithmic elasticity applied to the proposed control-cut object; not a newly discovered scaling law.
notes: No empirical value currently exists in this programme. Even log N cost diverges while elasticity tends to zero.

title: Adaptive Distributed Embodiment Resilience
core_claim: Survivors may re-coordinate after component loss. Evaluate scalar task recovery using \(C_k^*(G\setminus F)=\sup_{\pi\in\Pi(G\setminus F)}C_k(G\setminus F,\pi)\), and joint capability regions using the attainable set.
assumptions: Admissible recovery respects real controller state, compute, adaptation time, authorized access and resources. Coordinate maxima need not be jointly attainable.
falsifiers: Recovery fails, is too slow, is resource-limited, or depends on unavailable shared infrastructure. Sampled policies do not establish an optimal-response guarantee.
prior_art: Adaptive network interdiction; Prorok et al. (2021); Schlotfeldt et al. (2018); cross-embodiment adaptation.
notes: Actual adaptive-recovery performance must be measured. The formal envelope is a model definition, not an achieved capability.
